presentation: Positive patient identification for blood samples
stem:
A foundation doctor is asked to take a group and save sample from a man in bay 4 who is going to theatre in the afternoon. He is awake, alert and able to talk.

Before drawing any blood, which step is the most important?

options.A: Ask him 'Are you Mr Patel?' and then check the request form
options.B: Ask him to state his full name and date of birth and check these against his wristband and the form
options.C: Read the name written on the board above his bed
options.D: Pre-label the sample tubes at the nurses' station before going to the bedside
options.E: Confirm his identity using the bed number recorded on the request

correct_answer: B. Ask him to state his full name and date of birth and check these against his wristband and the form
why_correct: Positive patient identification is the first and most important safety step, because wrong-blood-in-tube errors can lead to misdiagnosis and fatal ABO-incompatible transfusion. An alert patient should be asked to state his own full name and date of birth, which are then checked against his wristband and the request form, and the tubes labelled at the bedside (SHOT; BSH guidance).
why_wrong: A. A closed question invites him to agree with the wrong name, especially if he is anxious or hard of hearing. C. Bed boards are unreliable and are not an accepted identifier. D. Labelling away from the patient is a leading cause of wrong-blood-in-tube incidents. E. Patients move beds, so bed numbers do not confirm identity.
pearl: Group and save samples should be labelled at the bedside immediately after collection, by hand or with a bedside label-printing system; pre-labelled tubes are a well-recognised cause of transfusion errors.
thinking: Pretransfusion sample needed ↓ Wrong-blood-in-tube can be fatal ↓ Alert patient states his own name and date of birth ↓ Cross-check wristband and request form ↓ Label at the bedside
exam_trap: A, Asking 'Are you Mr Patel?' — it seems to involve the patient, but a closed question can be answered 'yes' by the wrong person.
takeaway: Ask the patient to state their identifiers and match them to the wristband and request before taking blood.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl: BSH allows bedside label printers, not only handwritten labels; reworded.

stem:
A 79-year-old man with advanced age-related macular degeneration lives alone and manages his own tablets. At a GP review he is started on a new twice-daily medicine. He explains that he cannot read the printed dispensing labels or leaflets, even with a magnifier.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Ask his daughter to take over responsibility for his medicines
options.B: Change to a once-daily preparation so he does not need instructions
options.C: Delay starting the medicine until a carer can be present
options.D: Provide the instructions in a format he can use, such as large print, audio or braille labels
options.E: Hand him the standard printed information leaflet to keep

correct_answer: D. Provide the instructions in a format he can use, such as large print, audio or braille labels
why_correct: He is capable of managing his own medicines but needs information he can actually access. Under the NHS Accessible Information Standard and the Equality Act, services should record his communication needs and give instructions in a suitable format, for example large print, audio or braille labelling, with pharmacy support if needed.
why_wrong: A. Passing responsibility to a relative without his agreement removes his independence and is not required. B. Changing the regimen does not address his need for accessible information about any medicine. C. Delaying treatment because of a disability is discriminatory and unnecessary. E. Standard print is exactly what he has said he cannot read.
pearl: The Accessible Information Standard requires NHS services to identify, record, flag, share and meet patients' information and communication needs.
thinking: Capable patient managing own tablets ↓ Severe sight loss prevents reading labels ↓ Problem is format, not ability ↓ Make reasonable adjustments ↓ Provide accessible format instructions
exam_trap: A, Asking his daughter to manage his medicines — it seems a safe workaround, but it removes his autonomy without his consent when an accessible format would solve the problem.
takeaway: Adapt the format of information to the patient's needs rather than taking control away from them.

stem:
A 77-year-old woman attends her GP for a blood pressure check. She has capacity. When asked how things are at home, she becomes upset and says that her grandson, who moved in last year, has been taking money from her pension and she is scared to challenge him because he loses his temper.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Tell her that money matters are outside the GP's role
options.B: Take the disclosure seriously, assess her safety and follow adult safeguarding procedures with her involvement
options.C: Advise her to change her bank PIN and take no further action
options.D: Arrange a joint appointment to discuss it with her grandson present
options.E: Record the conversation in her notes but take no further action

correct_answer: B. Take the disclosure seriously, assess her safety and follow adult safeguarding procedures with her involvement
why_correct: Financial abuse is a recognised form of abuse under the Care Act 2014, and her fear of her grandson's temper raises concern about her wider safety. The GP should listen, check whether she is in immediate danger, explore her wishes and follow local adult safeguarding procedures. Because she has capacity, she should be involved in decisions, although information can still be shared without consent if there is a serious risk to her or others.
why_wrong: A. Financial abuse is a safeguarding issue and clinicians have a duty to respond. C. Practical advice alone leaves an adult at risk without support or protection. D. Discussing the allegation with the alleged abuser present could put her at greater risk. E. Documentation without action does nothing to protect her.
pearl: Financial or material abuse is one of the categories of abuse listed in the Care Act 2014 statutory guidance, alongside physical, sexual, psychological, neglect, discriminatory, organisational, domestic and modern slavery.
thinking: Older adult discloses money being taken ↓ Fear of the person responsible ↓ Financial abuse is a safeguarding category ↓ Assess immediate safety and her wishes ↓ Follow adult safeguarding procedures
exam_trap: E, Documenting and taking no action — recording the disclosure feels responsible, but on its own it leaves her exposed to ongoing abuse.
takeaway: A disclosure of financial abuse by an older adult needs a safeguarding response, not just advice or a note.

stem:
An 81-year-old man is being prepared for discharge from a medical ward after a chest infection. Staff notice that his nephew insists on holding his bank cards, answers every question for him and has asked twice when the house will be signed over. The patient has not raised any concerns himself, and there are no injuries.

What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Take no action because there is no physical injury
options.B: Speak with the patient alone about his safety, finances and wishes
options.C: Challenge the nephew about his behaviour at the bedside
options.D: Report the nephew to the police before speaking to the patient
options.E: Ask other relatives whether they share the staff's concerns

correct_answer: B. Speak with the patient alone about his safety, finances and wishes
why_correct: The concern is suspicion rather than disclosure, so the first step is a sensitive private conversation with the patient, away from the nephew. This allows the team to understand his wishes, check his capacity for financial decisions and assess his immediate safety before deciding on safeguarding action and a safe discharge plan.
why_wrong: A. Financial abuse rarely leaves physical signs, so the absence of injury is not reassuring. C. Confronting the nephew could escalate risk and make the patient less likely to speak openly. D. Police involvement may be needed later, but the patient's account and wishes should be explored first. E. Discussing concerns with other relatives without consent breaches confidentiality and may alert the suspected abuser.
pearl: An adult with capacity can make their own financial decisions, even unwise ones, but coercion or undue influence can undermine a decision and is a safeguarding matter.
thinking: Suspicion of financial abuse, no disclosure ↓ Controlling relative present at all times ↓ Need the patient's own account ↓ Speak to him alone ↓ Assess safety, wishes and capacity before acting
exam_trap: D, Reporting to the police straight away — it seems decisive, but without hearing from the patient himself the team does not know his account or wishes.
takeaway: When financial abuse is suspected, start by speaking to the patient privately about his safety and wishes.

stem:
A salaried GP sees a 40-year-old woman with a persistent, non-urgent skin eruption on her trunk that has not responded to emollients or a topical steroid. The GP does not recognise the pattern and is unsure what it is or how to treat it. There are no features suggesting cancer or a serious systemic illness.

What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Treat it based on an internet image search without involving anyone else
options.B: Tell her to find a private dermatologist herself
options.C: Seek specialist advice or refer her to a colleague with the relevant expertise
options.D: Make no decision and ask her to come back in six months
options.E: Start a course of oral steroids after reading about likely causes overnight

correct_answer: C. Seek specialist advice or refer her to a colleague with the relevant expertise
why_correct: Good medical practice requires doctors to recognise the limits of their competence and consult or refer when a problem falls outside them. The GP should discuss the case with a more experienced colleague or use specialist advice and guidance, referring to dermatology if needed, so that she is assessed by someone with the right expertise.
why_wrong: A. Acting on an image search alone is unsafe and outside the doctor's competence. B. The GP remains responsible for arranging appropriate help rather than leaving her to organise it. D. An unexplained, persistent rash should not be left unmanaged for months. E. Reading overnight does not provide competence, and empirical oral steroids may cause harm or mask the diagnosis.
pearl: Advice and guidance services allow GPs to obtain specialist input without a full referral, often avoiding an outpatient appointment.
thinking: Problem outside the GP's experience ↓ Not urgent but unresolved ↓ Recognise limits of competence ↓ Consult a colleague or specialist ↓ Refer if needed
exam_trap: E, Starting oral steroids after self-study — it feels proactive, but reading does not create competence and blind treatment can obscure the diagnosis.
takeaway: When a problem is beyond your competence, seek advice from or refer to someone who has the expertise.

stem:
At 2 am a foundation doctor on a surgical ward is called to a man two days after bowel surgery. He is newly confused, cold and clammy, with a rising heart rate and falling blood pressure. The doctor has started an ABCDE assessment but feels out of their depth and unsure what to do next.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Manage him alone overnight to gain experience
options.B: Hand over to the day team at the morning ward round
options.C: Ask another foundation doctor for ideas rather than escalate
options.D: Record the findings and plan a repeat review in four hours
options.E: Call for senior help now while continuing immediate assessment and treatment

correct_answer: E. Call for senior help now while continuing immediate assessment and treatment
why_correct: He shows signs of shock after major surgery and could deteriorate rapidly. A doctor who is unsure how to manage the situation must escalate early to a senior while continuing ABCDE assessment and initial treatment, as required by GMC Good medical practice and the NEWS2 escalation framework.
why_wrong: A. Working beyond one's competence puts an unstable patient at risk. B. Waiting until morning allows the shock to progress. C. A colleague at the same level cannot replace senior review. D. A four-hour delay is unsafe in a patient with signs of circulatory compromise.
pearl: Under NEWS2, an aggregate score of 7 or more should trigger an emergency response from a team with critical care competencies, while a score of 5 or 6, or a single parameter scoring 3, needs urgent clinical review.
thinking: Postoperative patient deteriorating ↓ Signs of shock ↓ Junior doctor unsure of next steps ↓ Escalate to senior early ↓ Continue ABCDE care while help arrives
exam_trap: C, Asking another foundation doctor — it feels like seeking help, but advice from someone equally inexperienced does not provide the senior input an unstable patient needs.
takeaway: When a patient is deteriorating and you are unsure, call for senior help early and keep treating.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl misstated NEWS2: single red parameter = urgent clinical review, 7+ = emergency/critical care response; corrected.

stem:
On a busy medical take, a registrar asks a first-year foundation doctor to carry out a diagnostic lumbar puncture alone while the registrar sees other patients. The foundation doctor has watched the procedure once but has never performed it or been trained in it.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Go ahead carefully and write in the notes that it is a first attempt
options.B: Do it because the registrar has asked and is responsible
options.C: Read the trust procedure guide and then perform it unsupervised
options.D: Explain the lack of training and ask for supervision or for a competent clinician to perform it
options.E: Watch an online video of the technique before starting alone

correct_answer: D. Explain the lack of training and ask for supervision or for a competent clinician to perform it
why_correct: Doctors must work within the limits of their competence. Being asked by a senior does not transfer that responsibility, so the foundation doctor should explain honestly that they are not trained and ask either to be supervised or for someone competent to do it, which also serves as a training opportunity.
why_wrong: A. Documenting a first attempt does not make an unsupervised, untrained procedure safe. B. A senior's request does not override the duty to work within competence. C. Reading a guide is not training and does not confer competence. E. A video cannot replace supervised practice.
pearl: GMC Good medical practice states that doctors must recognise and work within the limits of their competence, even when a more senior colleague asks them to act.
thinking: Asked to do an untrained procedure ↓ Senior request does not transfer responsibility ↓ Patient safety comes first ↓ Explain limitation honestly ↓ Request supervision or a competent operator
exam_trap: B, Doing it because the registrar asked — hierarchy makes it feel expected, but each doctor remains responsible for working within their own competence.
takeaway: Never perform an untrained procedure alone; say so and get supervision or a competent colleague.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman with ileal Crohn's disease diagnosed ten years ago attends the emergency department with her fourth episode in a few months of colicky central abdominal pain after meals, followed by vomiting and bloating that settles after a day or two. She has no fever and her inflammatory markers are only mildly raised.

Which complication best explains her symptoms?

options.A: Fibrotic ileal stricture causing intermittent small bowel obstruction

correct_answer: A. Fibrotic ileal stricture causing intermittent small bowel obstruction
why_correct: Long-standing transmural inflammation in Crohn's disease heals with fibrosis, narrowing the bowel lumen, most often in the terminal ileum. This produces recurrent post-prandial colicky pain, vomiting and distension from partial obstruction. Only mildly raised markers suggest a predominantly fibrotic rather than active inflammatory narrowing, which may need endoscopic dilatation or surgery.
why_wrong: B. A perianal abscess causes local pain, swelling and fever rather than obstructive symptoms. C. Toxic megacolon is an acute colonic emergency with systemic toxicity, not recurrent self-settling episodes. D. Gallstone ileus is a rare cause of obstruction in older women and would not recur in this pattern. E. An enterovesical fistula causes pneumaturia, faecaluria and recurrent urinary infections.
pearl: MR enterography is the usual imaging for assessing small bowel Crohn's strictures because it avoids radiation in young patients who may need repeated scans.
thinking: Long-standing ileal Crohn's disease ↓ Recurrent colicky pain after meals ↓ Vomiting and bloating that settle ↓ Low inflammatory activity ↓ Fibrotic stricture with partial obstruction
exam_trap: C, Toxic megacolon — it is a well-known IBD complication, but it is a colonic emergency with systemic toxicity rather than recurring episodes of post-prandial obstruction.
takeaway: Recurrent obstructive symptoms in long-standing Crohn's disease suggest a stricture.

stem:
A 41-year-old man with a known diagnosis of extensive ulcerative colitis is admitted with a flare. On the third day he becomes drowsy and febrile, his abdomen becomes tense and tender, and his bowel frequency paradoxically falls. He is tachycardic. A plain abdominal film shows a grossly dilated transverse colon with loss of haustral markings.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Toxic megacolon is a life-threatening complication of severe colitis in which the colon dilates, typically the transverse colon, and the patient becomes systemically toxic. A falling stool frequency in this context is ominous rather than reassuring. It needs urgent senior medical and surgical review, with colectomy if there is no rapid response or if perforation occurs.
why_wrong: A. Sigmoid volvulus usually affects older, constipated patients and shows a coffee-bean loop arising from the pelvis. C. Pseudo-obstruction occurs in frail or post-operative patients without systemic toxicity from colitis. D. Adhesional obstruction causes dilated small bowel loops, usually after previous surgery. E. Perforated diverticulitis presents with peritonitis and free gas rather than a dilated transverse colon in a patient with colitis.
pearl: Toxic megacolon is defined radiologically as a colonic diameter over about 6 cm with systemic toxicity; steroids can mask signs of perforation.
thinking: Known ulcerative colitis in acute flare ↓ Fever, tachycardia, drowsiness ↓ Fewer stools with distension ↓ Dilated transverse colon, lost haustra ↓ Toxic megacolon
exam_trap: C, Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction — it also produces massive colonic dilatation, but it is not accompanied by systemic toxicity from an active colitis.
takeaway: Severe colitis with systemic toxicity and a dilated colon is toxic megacolon until proved otherwise.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman with alcohol-related liver cirrhosis and known ascites is seen in the medical admissions unit. Over two days she has developed a low-grade temperature, diffuse abdominal tenderness and mild new confusion, and her ascites has increased.

Which investigation is the most important to perform without delay?

options.B: CT of the abdomen with contrast
options.C: Diagnostic paracentesis for ascitic fluid analysis
options.E: Abdominal ultrasound to measure liver size

correct_answer: C. Diagnostic paracentesis for ascitic fluid analysis
why_correct: Fever, abdominal tenderness and worsening encephalopathy in a patient with cirrhotic ascites should be treated as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis until proved otherwise. A diagnostic tap for neutrophil count, culture and other analysis is the key test, and British Society of Gastroenterology guidance advises a diagnostic tap in everyone with cirrhosis and ascites who is admitted, so that antibiotics can be started promptly if confirmed.
why_wrong: A. Endoscopy looks for varices but does not investigate infected ascites. B. CT may help if secondary peritonitis is suspected but does not diagnose spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. D. Ammonia levels add little to the clinical assessment of encephalopathy and do not identify its cause. E. Measuring liver size does not answer whether the ascites is infected.
pearl: An ascitic neutrophil count above 250 cells per cubic millimetre is diagnostic of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
thinking: Cirrhosis with ascites ↓ Fever, abdominal tenderness, new confusion ↓ Suspect spontaneous bacterial peritonitis ↓ Diagnostic tap for neutrophil count and culture ↓ Start antibiotics promptly
exam_trap: D, Serum ammonia — the confusion tempts a focus on hepatic encephalopathy, but the encephalopathy here is likely being triggered by infection that needs diagnosing.
takeaway: Any deterioration in a patient with cirrhotic ascites warrants a diagnostic ascitic tap to look for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
notes: Reviewer fix: Diagnostic tap on admission attributed to NICE NG50; corrected attribution to BSG ascites guidance.

stem:
A 46-year-old woman is admitted with severe epigastric pain radiating through to her back and a markedly raised serum amylase. She is a lifelong teetotaller and takes no regular medicines. She mentions several previous bouts of right upper abdominal pain after fatty meals, and her liver function tests show a raised ALT. Calcium and lipids are normal.

What is the most likely underlying cause?
why_correct: Gallstones and alcohol are the two commonest causes of acute pancreatitis in the UK. With no alcohol intake, previous biliary-type pain and a raised ALT, gallstone pancreatitis is by far the most likely. NICE NG104 advises abdominal ultrasound to look for gallstones and, where they are found, early cholecystectomy, during the same admission where appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Hypertriglyceridaemia is an uncommon cause and her lipids are normal. B. She takes no regular medicines. D. Her calcium is normal. E. Autoimmune pancreatitis is rare and there is nothing pointing to it here.
pearl: A raised ALT early in acute pancreatitis strongly suggests a gallstone cause.
thinking: Acute pancreatitis confirmed ↓ No alcohol excess or drugs ↓ Previous biliary colic ↓ Raised ALT ↓ Gallstone pancreatitis: arrange ultrasound
exam_trap: A, Hypertriglyceridaemia — it is a classic textbook cause when alcohol is absent, but it is uncommon and her lipid profile is normal.
takeaway: In acute pancreatitis without alcohol excess, look for gallstones first.
notes: Reviewer fix: Removed 'or within two weeks' cholecystectomy timing; now 'early, same admission where appropriate' (NICE NG104).

stem:
For the past eight months, a 31-year-old warehouse manager has had cramping discomfort low in his belly with a swollen, gassy feeling. Some weeks he is loose, other weeks he struggles to go, and going to the toilet relieves the cramps. Busy shifts make it flare. He has kept his weight, seen no blood and sleeps undisturbed. His GP finds normal haematology, CRP, tissue transglutaminase antibodies and faecal calprotectin.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Abdominal pain relieved by defecation with altered bowel habit and bloating for over six months, without red-flag features, fits irritable bowel syndrome. NICE CG61 recommends checking a full blood count, inflammatory markers and coeliac serology, and a normal faecal calprotectin helps exclude inflammatory bowel disease, allowing a positive diagnosis.
why_wrong: B. Negative coeliac serology makes coeliac disease unlikely. C. A normal calprotectin and CRP with no weight loss or bleeding argue against Crohn's disease. D. Microscopic colitis typically causes persistent watery diarrhoea in older adults, not alternating habit. E. Bile acid diarrhoea causes chronic watery diarrhoea rather than alternating constipation and loose stools.
pearl: Faecal calprotectin is used in primary care to distinguish irritable bowel syndrome from inflammatory bowel disease in adults under 40 with lower gastrointestinal symptoms.
thinking: Pain relieved by defecation ↓ Alternating bowel habit and bloating ↓ No red flags ↓ Normal bloods, coeliac serology and calprotectin ↓ Irritable bowel syndrome
exam_trap: D, Microscopic colitis — it causes bowel symptoms with normal bloods, but it produces persistent watery diarrhoea, usually in older people, not an alternating pattern.
takeaway: Pain eased by defecation, altered habit and no red flags with normal tests point to irritable bowel syndrome.
notes: Reviewer fix: Stem 'since the spring' gave no duration; set eight months to match the >6-month IBS criterion in why_correct.

stem:
A 72-year-old woman tells her GP she has had intermittent cramping pain in the left lower abdomen for several months, with bloating and a tendency to constipation. She has no fever and is not unwell between episodes. Her CRP is normal. A recent colonoscopy showed numerous sigmoid diverticula with no inflammation, bleeding or tumour.

Which term best describes her condition?
why_correct: NICE NG147 distinguishes three terms. Diverticulosis means diverticula without symptoms; diverticular disease means diverticula causing symptoms such as intermittent lower abdominal pain and altered bowel habit, without inflammation; and diverticulitis means inflammation or infection of the diverticula. She has symptoms, diverticula and no evidence of inflammation, so she has diverticular disease.
why_wrong: A. Diverticulosis applies only when the diverticula are asymptomatic. B. Acute diverticulitis would cause constant pain with fever, raised inflammatory markers or inflamed bowel on imaging. C. Ischaemic colitis causes sudden pain with bloody diarrhoea and abnormal mucosa. D. Her symptoms are explained by the diverticula found, so a diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome is not the best description.
pearl: NICE NG147 advises a healthy balanced diet including whole grains, fruit and vegetables for people with diverticular disease, with bulk-forming laxatives for persistent constipation.
thinking: Diverticula seen in the sigmoid ↓ She has symptoms, so not diverticulosis ↓ No fever, normal CRP, no inflammation ↓ Not diverticulitis ↓ Diverticular disease
exam_trap: A, Diverticulosis — it is the familiar term for diverticula seen on imaging, but it is reserved for patients without symptoms.
takeaway: Symptomatic diverticula without inflammation are called diverticular disease.

stem:
A 46-year-old woman is admitted from the emergency department with severe upper abdominal pain boring through to her back and a markedly raised serum lipase. Over the past year she has seen her GP several times with bouts of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, each settling within a few hours. She drinks alcohol only occasionally and takes no regular medicines.

What is the most likely underlying cause of her current illness?
why_correct: Gallstones are the leading cause of acute pancreatitis in the UK. Her repeated episodes of post-prandial right upper quadrant pain are typical biliary colic, so a stone passing into the common bile duct and obstructing the pancreatic duct is the most likely trigger. An abdominal ultrasound should be arranged to look for stones and bile duct dilatation.
why_wrong: A. She drinks only occasionally, so alcohol is unlikely to be responsible. B. Very high triglycerides can cause pancreatitis, but nothing here suggests it and her history points to biliary disease. D. Hypercalcaemia is a rare cause and there are no features of it. E. She takes no regular medicines.
pearl: Patients with gallstone pancreatitis should have cholecystectomy during the same admission or within two weeks, because recurrence is common while the gallbladder remains.
thinking: Severe epigastric pain to the back with raised lipase ↓ Acute pancreatitis ↓ Prior recurrent post-prandial RUQ pain suggests biliary colic ↓ Minimal alcohol and no drugs ↓ Gallstones most likely cause
exam_trap: A, Alcohol excess — it is the other common cause and is often reached for reflexively, but her alcohol intake is minimal and her biliary history points elsewhere.
takeaway: Acute pancreatitis in someone with recurrent biliary colic is gallstone pancreatitis until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 27-year-old man sees his GP with several months of crampy lower abdominal pain and an erratic bowel habit. He also mentions low back stiffness that is worst on waking and eases with exercise, and last week tender, raised, purple-red lumps appeared on the front of both lower legs.

Which diagnosis best explains all of his symptoms?
why_correct: Crohn's disease is an inflammatory bowel disease that commonly has extraintestinal manifestations. The tender shin nodules are erythema nodosum, and morning back stiffness easing with activity suggests an inflammatory enteropathic spondyloarthritis. Together with chronic abdominal pain and altered bowel habit in a young adult, this points to Crohn's disease, and faecal calprotectin with gastroenterology referral is appropriate.
why_wrong: B. Irritable bowel syndrome is a functional disorder and does not cause erythema nodosum or inflammatory back pain. C. Coeliac disease causes malabsorption features and is not typically linked with erythema nodosum and spondyloarthritis. D. Diverticular disease is unusual at this age and lacks these systemic features. E. Peptic ulcer disease causes epigastric pain and does not explain the skin or joint findings.
pearl: Erythema nodosum and peripheral arthritis tend to flare with bowel disease activity, whereas axial spondyloarthritis and uveitis often run an independent course.
thinking: Young adult with chronic abdominal pain and altered bowel habit ↓ Tender red shin nodules = erythema nodosum ↓ Inflammatory-pattern back pain ↓ Extraintestinal manifestations imply inflammatory bowel disease ↓ Crohn's disease
exam_trap: B, Irritable bowel syndrome — the bowel symptoms alone could fit, but IBS never explains objective inflammatory features such as erythema nodosum or inflammatory back pain.
takeaway: Bowel symptoms with erythema nodosum or inflammatory back pain should prompt consideration of inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn's.

stem:
A 55-year-old woman attends the emergency department after a night of repeated vomiting. Her serum lipase is several times the upper limit of normal. Before labelling this as acute pancreatitis, the registrar wants a clinical feature that fits the diagnosis.

Which finding in her history would best support it?

options.A: Intermittent colicky right loin pain spreading to the groin
options.B: Painless yellowing of the skin with a palpable gallbladder
options.C: Fresh red blood mixed in with her stools
options.D: Constant severe upper abdominal pain radiating through to the back
options.E: Sharp central chest pain eased by sitting forward

correct_answer: D. Constant severe upper abdominal pain radiating through to the back
why_correct: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when two of three criteria are met: characteristic abdominal pain, amylase or lipase at least three times the upper limit of normal, and typical imaging findings. She already has the biochemical criterion, so constant severe epigastric pain radiating to the back would complete the clinical picture and make imaging unnecessary for diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Colicky loin-to-groin pain suggests renal colic. B. Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder suggests malignant distal bile duct obstruction such as pancreatic head cancer. C. Fresh blood in the stools points to a lower gastrointestinal source. E. Pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward suggests pericarditis.
pearl: The height of amylase or lipase does not correlate with severity; severity is judged by organ failure and scoring systems such as the Glasgow-Imrie criteria.
thinking: Lipase raised more than three-fold ↓ Diagnosis needs two of three criteria ↓ Need typical pain or imaging ↓ Constant epigastric pain to the back is the typical pain ↓ Supports acute pancreatitis
exam_trap: B, Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder — it is a pancreatic-sounding finding, but it suggests pancreatic head malignancy rather than acute pancreatitis.
takeaway: Acute pancreatitis is confirmed by typical epigastric pain plus enzymes at least three times normal, or imaging if either is missing.

stem:
A 17-year-old boy is reviewed in the GP surgery. On several occasions over the past year, within minutes of eating prawns, he has developed cramping abdominal pain, loose stools, itchy lips and a tight chest with audible wheeze. Each episode has settled within a few hours, he has never had a fever, and he is entirely well in between.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Rapid onset of gut symptoms together with oral itching and wheeze after a specific food, resolving between exposures, is typical of IgE-mediated food allergy. Involvement of the respiratory tract means he is at risk of anaphylaxis, so he needs referral to an allergy service, advice on strict avoidance and consideration of adrenaline auto-injectors.
why_wrong: B. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause wheeze or oral itching. C. Coeliac disease produces chronic symptoms rather than rapid reactions within minutes, and does not cause wheeze. D. Lactose intolerance causes bloating and diarrhoea after dairy, not wheeze after shellfish. E. Infective gastroenteritis would not recur reproducibly within minutes of one food, and would usually cause fever.
pearl: Shellfish, peanuts and tree nuts are common causes of IgE-mediated allergy that usually persists into adult life.
thinking: Symptoms within minutes of a specific food ↓ Gut plus skin plus respiratory involvement ↓ Well between episodes, no fever ↓ Immediate hypersensitivity reaction ↓ IgE-mediated food allergy
exam_trap: D, Lactose intolerance — food-triggered diarrhoea and cramps tempt a diagnosis of intolerance, but intolerance never causes wheeze or lip itching.
takeaway: Food-triggered gut symptoms with wheeze or oral itching within minutes indicate IgE-mediated allergy with anaphylaxis risk.

stem:
A 26-year-old man has had a year of cramping lower abdominal pain that eases after opening his bowels, with bloating and loose stools on bad days. He feels better when he cuts down on bread and pasta. Coeliac blood tests were sent while he was eating gluten daily and were negative, with a normal total IgA. His weight, full blood count and examination are normal and he has had no rectal bleeding.

Which diagnosis best explains his symptoms?
why_correct: NICE supports a positive diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome when abdominal pain relieved by defecation occurs with bloating or altered stool form, and there are no red flags. Coeliac disease has been reasonably excluded because serology was taken on adequate gluten intake with normal total IgA. Symptom improvement on cutting wheat is common in IBS, as wheat is rich in fermentable carbohydrates.
why_wrong: A. Negative tTG with normal total IgA taken during gluten intake makes coeliac disease very unlikely. B. Crohn's disease would usually produce weight loss, anaemia or raised inflammatory markers. D. Colorectal cancer is very unlikely at this age without weight loss, anaemia or bleeding. E. Chronic pancreatitis causes epigastric pain and steatorrhoea, usually with heavy alcohol use.
pearl: Faecal calprotectin is recommended in adults under 40 with lower gut symptoms to help distinguish IBS from inflammatory bowel disease.
thinking: Pain relieved by defecation with bloating and loose stools ↓ No weight loss, anaemia or bleeding ↓ Coeliac serology negative on gluten with normal IgA ↓ Organic causes not supported ↓ Irritable bowel syndrome
exam_trap: A, Coeliac disease — improvement on avoiding bread is tempting, but properly timed negative serology with normal total IgA largely excludes it.
takeaway: IBS can be diagnosed positively once red flags are absent and coeliac disease has been excluded by correctly timed serology.

stem:
A 38-year-old man tells the practice nurse that on some days he gets bloating, cramps and loose stools after meals, and he wonders whether he is intolerant of something in his diet. Between episodes he feels well, and he has no weight loss or bleeding.

Which part of the history will be most helpful in assessing a possible food intolerance?

options.C: The timing of symptoms in relation to particular foods eaten
options.D: Any family history of hearing loss

correct_answer: C. The timing of symptoms in relation to particular foods eaten
why_correct: Assessing food intolerance relies on identifying which foods precede symptoms, how soon after eating they start, and whether they are reproducible. A food and symptom diary is a practical way to capture this. This history guides any trial of exclusion and helps separate intolerance from allergy or other gut disease.
why_wrong: A. Blood group has no role in diagnosing food intolerance. B. Vaccination history does not help identify a dietary trigger. D. Family history of hearing loss is unrelated to gut symptoms. E. Previous sports injuries are irrelevant to food-related symptoms.
pearl: Unlike IgE-mediated allergy, food intolerance is usually dose-related and delayed, and there is no reliable blood test for it.
thinking: Episodic gut symptoms after meals ↓ Well between episodes, no alarm features ↓ Possible food intolerance ↓ Diagnosis rests on linking specific foods to symptoms ↓ Take a food and symptom timing history
exam_trap: A, ABO blood group — blood-type diets are popular, but blood group has no evidence base in assessing food intolerance.
takeaway: The key to assessing food intolerance is a careful history linking specific foods to the timing of symptoms.

stem:
A 34-year-old man phones the GP surgery. He has noticed bloating and loose stools after meals containing bread, and a friend has told him to go gluten-free straight away. The GP thinks coeliac disease is possible. He is still eating his normal diet.

What should the GP advise?

options.A: Start a strict gluten-free diet now and test only if symptoms persist
options.B: Keep eating gluten and have coeliac blood tests before changing his diet
options.C: Cut out all carbohydrates for a month to see if symptoms settle
options.D: Take a short course of oral prednisolone

correct_answer: B. Keep eating gluten and have coeliac blood tests before changing his diet
why_correct: Coeliac serology and duodenal biopsy depend on ongoing gluten exposure, so excluding gluten before testing can produce false-negative results. NICE advises that people should eat gluten in more than one meal every day for at least six weeks before testing. He should therefore continue his usual diet and have tTG IgA with total IgA checked first.
why_wrong: A. Going gluten-free first risks a false-negative result and leaves the diagnosis uncertain. C. Removing all carbohydrates is unnecessary and does not help confirm the diagnosis. D. Steroids are not used for suspected coeliac disease. E. There is nothing to suggest a surgical emergency.
pearl: If someone has already gone gluten-free, they need a gluten challenge before serology is reliable.
thinking: Possible coeliac disease ↓ Tests rely on immune response to gluten ↓ Excluding gluten first causes false negatives ↓ He is still eating gluten ↓ Test now before any dietary change
exam_trap: A, Starting a gluten-free diet now — it seems a sensible low-risk trial, but it undermines serology and can leave the diagnosis permanently unclear.
takeaway: Test for coeliac disease while the person is still eating gluten, before any dietary exclusion.

stem:
A 21-year-old woman sees her GP with four months of crampy abdominal pain and loose stools. She feels exhausted most of the time, and her clothes have become loose although she has not been trying to diet.

Which feature of her history most strongly suggests an organic bowel disorder rather than irritable bowel syndrome?

options.A: Pain that eases after a bowel movement
options.B: Bloating that worsens as the day goes on
options.C: Symptoms that vary from day to day
options.D: Passing stools more often than usual

why_correct: Unintentional weight loss is a red flag that should not be attributed to irritable bowel syndrome. In a young woman with diarrhoea and fatigue it raises the possibility of inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease, so she needs blood tests, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin rather than a label of IBS.
why_wrong: A. Pain relieved by defecation is a typical IBS feature. B. Bloating, often worse later in the day, is common in IBS. C. Fluctuating symptoms are characteristic of IBS. D. Increased stool frequency on its own occurs in IBS and is not a red flag.
pearl: Other features that argue against IBS include rectal bleeding, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia, raised inflammatory markers and a family history of bowel or ovarian cancer.
thinking: Chronic abdominal pain with loose stools ↓ IBS is common but a diagnosis of exclusion of red flags ↓ Unintentional weight loss is a red flag ↓ Suggests organic disease such as IBD or coeliac ↓ Investigate rather than label IBS
exam_trap: D, Passing stools more often — a change in bowel habit sounds worrying, but increased frequency alone is part of IBS and is not an alarm feature.
takeaway: Unintentional weight loss should never be explained away as irritable bowel syndrome.

stem:
A 63-year-old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis is admitted to the medical ward with increasing abdominal swelling, a fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness. She has become slightly muddled over the past day.

Which investigation is essential to confirm the most likely cause of her deterioration?

options.C: Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic neutrophil count and culture

correct_answer: C. Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic neutrophil count and culture
why_correct: Fever, abdominal tenderness and new confusion in a patient with cirrhotic ascites suggest spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. The diagnosis is made by a diagnostic ascitic tap, with an ascitic neutrophil count above the diagnostic threshold and fluid sent in blood culture bottles. The tap should be done promptly, ideally before antibiotics, as SBP carries high mortality.
why_wrong: A. Amylase assesses pancreatitis, which does not explain infected ascites. B. CT may show ascites but cannot diagnose peritoneal infection. D. Endoscopy is for varices and upper GI bleeding. E. Ammonia levels do not establish the cause of encephalopathy and do not diagnose infection.
pearl: Every patient with cirrhosis and ascites admitted to hospital should have a diagnostic paracentesis, even without abdominal symptoms, because SBP is often silent.
thinking: Cirrhosis with ascites ↓ Fever, abdominal tenderness and new confusion ↓ Suspect spontaneous bacterial peritonitis ↓ Diagnosis depends on ascitic fluid analysis ↓ Diagnostic paracentesis
exam_trap: E, Blood ammonia — confusion in cirrhosis suggests hepatic encephalopathy, but the encephalopathy is being driven by infection, which only an ascitic tap will confirm.
takeaway: Suspected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed by ascitic fluid neutrophil count and culture from a diagnostic tap.

stem:
A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis due to hepatitis C has routine bloods at his liver clinic review. His platelet count has fallen steadily over two years, while his haemoglobin and white cell count remain close to normal. On examination the spleen tip is palpable. He has no bleeding symptoms and takes no new medicines.

What is the most likely mechanism of his low platelet count?

options.C: Pooling of platelets in an enlarged spleen due to portal hypertension

correct_answer: C. Pooling of platelets in an enlarged spleen due to portal hypertension
why_correct: Cirrhosis raises pressure in the portal venous system, causing congestive splenomegaly. The enlarged spleen sequesters platelets (hypersplenism), so a gradually falling platelet count with a palpable spleen in liver disease is most likely due to portal hypertension. Reduced hepatic thrombopoietin production can contribute.
why_wrong: A. Marrow infiltration would usually affect other cell lines and does not explain splenomegaly. B. Immune thrombocytopenia is a diagnosis of exclusion and does not cause splenomegaly. D. Folate deficiency would typically cause macrocytic anaemia too. E. DIC is an acute illness with bleeding and deranged clotting, not a slow decline in a well patient.
pearl: A low platelet count is often the earliest blood clue to portal hypertension and is used, with liver stiffness, to decide who needs variceal screening.
thinking: Cirrhosis ↓ Slowly falling platelets with other counts preserved ↓ Palpable spleen ↓ Portal hypertension causes splenic congestion ↓ Hypersplenism sequesters platelets
exam_trap: B, Immune thrombocytopenia — isolated low platelets suggest ITP, but the cirrhosis and splenomegaly give a clear alternative explanation.
takeaway: Thrombocytopenia with splenomegaly in chronic liver disease usually reflects hypersplenism from portal hypertension.

stem:
A 61-year-old woman has a mildly raised ALT on two blood tests six months apart, found during a medication review. She feels well and drinks very little alcohol. She mentions that she needed a blood transfusion after a complicated delivery in the 1980s.

Which infection should be tested for?
why_correct: Hepatitis C is a blood-borne virus that becomes chronic in most people and can remain silent for decades while causing persistently raised transaminases. UK blood donations were not screened for hepatitis C until 1991, so anyone transfused before then should be offered testing. Hepatitis C antibody with confirmatory RNA testing is appropriate, as curative antiviral treatment is available.
why_wrong: A. Hepatitis A is spread faeco-orally and causes only acute infection. B. Hepatitis E is usually acute and self-limiting, becoming chronic mainly in immunosuppressed people. C. Epstein-Barr virus causes acute hepatitis with glandular fever, not years of silent enzyme rise. E. Cytomegalovirus does not cause chronic hepatitis in immunocompetent adults.
pearl: Direct-acting antivirals cure hepatitis C in over 95% of patients after a short oral course.
thinking: Persistently raised ALT in a well patient ↓ Blood transfusion before 1991 ↓ Blood-borne virus that becomes chronic ↓ Can be silent for decades ↓ Test for hepatitis C
exam_trap: B, Hepatitis E — it can be transmitted by blood and can become chronic, but chronic infection is largely confined to immunosuppressed patients.
takeaway: Persistently raised liver enzymes with a pre-1991 transfusion should prompt testing for hepatitis C.

stem:
A 69-year-old man who had a right hemicolectomy for caecal adenocarcinoma 18 months ago attends his surveillance appointment. He has lost weight and his liver blood tests have become deranged. CT shows several rounded lesions scattered through both lobes of the liver.

What is the most likely explanation?

options.B: Metastatic spread of his bowel cancer to the liver

correct_answer: B. Metastatic spread of his bowel cancer to the liver
why_correct: The liver is the commonest site of distant spread from colorectal cancer because venous blood from the bowel drains through the portal vein to the liver. Multiple lesions in both lobes, new deranged liver tests and weight loss in a man with previous bowel cancer make metastases most likely. He needs multidisciplinary review, as some colorectal liver metastases can be resected.
why_wrong: A. Hepatocellular carcinoma usually arises in a cirrhotic liver and is often a single dominant mass. C. Simple cysts are benign and do not cause weight loss or deranged liver tests. D. Liver abscesses usually present with fever and rigors. E. Haemangiomas are common benign incidental lesions and do not cause weight loss.
pearl: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is used in colorectal cancer follow-up to monitor for recurrence, not for screening.
thinking: Previous colorectal cancer ↓ Weight loss and new deranged liver tests ↓ Multiple liver lesions in both lobes ↓ Portal venous drainage carries tumour to the liver ↓ Liver metastases
exam_trap: A, Hepatocellular carcinoma — a liver tumour is the obvious word, but multiple lesions in a non-cirrhotic liver after bowel cancer point to secondary, not primary, disease.
takeaway: New liver lesions after colorectal cancer are metastases until proven otherwise.

stem:
A hepatologist reviewing a man with long-standing cirrhosis wants a blood test that reflects how well the liver has been making proteins over the past few weeks, rather than over the past day or two.

Which test is most useful for this purpose?
why_correct: Albumin is made only by the liver and has a half-life of around three weeks, so a low level reflects reduced synthetic capacity over a longer period. This makes it useful for tracking chronic liver dysfunction, and it forms part of the Child-Pugh score. It can also be lowered by malnutrition, sepsis and protein loss, so it must be interpreted in context.
why_wrong: A. The prothrombin time reflects clotting factors with half-lives of hours, so it measures short-term synthetic function. B. ALT reflects hepatocyte injury, not synthetic function. D. Alkaline phosphatase indicates cholestasis or bone turnover. E. Creatine kinase is a marker of muscle injury.
pearl: Because clotting factor VII has a half-life of only a few hours, the INR is the best early marker of deteriorating synthetic function in acute liver failure.
thinking: Wants a measure of liver protein synthesis ↓ Over weeks rather than days ↓ Needs a long half-life liver-made protein ↓ INR is short-term ↓ Albumin
exam_trap: A, Prothrombin time — it is a true synthetic marker, but it reflects short-lived clotting factors and so changes over hours to days, not weeks.
takeaway: Albumin reflects longer-term hepatic synthetic function, whereas the INR reflects acute changes.

presentation: Prolonged prothrombin time in liver disease
stem:
A 52-year-old woman with decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis is found on admission bloods to have a prolonged prothrombin time. She takes no anticoagulant, and the result does not improve after intravenous vitamin K.

Which process does this result most directly reflect?

options.A: Platelet sequestration in an enlarged spleen
options.C: Reduced hepatic production of clotting factors

correct_answer: C. Reduced hepatic production of clotting factors
why_correct: The liver synthesises most clotting factors, including factors II, VII, IX and X. When hepatocyte function fails, their production falls and the prothrombin time lengthens. Failure to correct with vitamin K shows the problem is synthetic failure rather than vitamin K deficiency, which is why the INR is a key prognostic marker in liver disease.
why_wrong: A. Splenic sequestration lowers the platelet count but does not affect the prothrombin time. B. Haemolysis does not prolong the prothrombin time. D. Marrow suppression lowers blood cell counts but does not alter clotting factor levels. E. Pancreatic enzymes have no role in clotting factor synthesis.
pearl: A prolonged prothrombin time that corrects with vitamin K suggests cholestasis or malnutrition rather than hepatocellular failure.
thinking: Prolonged prothrombin time in cirrhosis ↓ No anticoagulant ↓ No correction with vitamin K ↓ Not vitamin K deficiency ↓ Impaired hepatic clotting factor synthesis
exam_trap: A, Platelet sequestration — hypersplenism causes bleeding risk in cirrhosis, but platelets are not measured by the prothrombin time.
takeaway: A prolonged prothrombin time in liver disease that does not correct with vitamin K reflects failing clotting factor synthesis.

presentation: Primary sclerosing cholangitis and ulcerative colitis
stem:
A 33-year-old man with ulcerative colitis, well controlled on mesalazine, is found at his annual review to have a persistently raised alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase with near-normal transaminases. He has no symptoms.

Which liver condition is most likely?
why_correct: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is a chronic inflammatory stricturing disease of the bile ducts that produces a cholestatic picture. Most patients with PSC have inflammatory bowel disease, usually ulcerative colitis, and it is more common in men. The next step is MRCP to look for multifocal bile duct strictures.
why_wrong: A. Primary biliary cholangitis is cholestatic but mainly affects middle-aged women and is not particularly associated with IBD. C. Autoimmune hepatitis causes a hepatitic picture with raised transaminases. D. Haemochromatosis causes iron overload with raised ferritin rather than isolated cholestasis. E. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal enzymes.
pearl: People with PSC and colitis have a much higher risk of colorectal cancer and need annual surveillance colonoscopy from diagnosis.
thinking: Ulcerative colitis ↓ Persistently raised ALP and GGT ↓ Cholestatic pattern ↓ Young man with IBD ↓ Primary sclerosing cholangitis
exam_trap: A, Primary biliary cholangitis — it is the other classic cholestatic autoimmune disease, but it typically affects middle-aged women and lacks the strong IBD link.
takeaway: A cholestatic liver picture in someone with ulcerative colitis should raise suspicion of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

stem:
A 57-year-old man has type 2 diabetes, a greyish-bronze tan that he has all year round, and an enlarged liver. Genetic testing shows he is homozygous for the C282Y mutation in the HFE gene.

What process underlies his condition?

options.A: Excessive intestinal absorption of iron with deposition in organs
options.D: Autoimmune destruction of small bile ducts

correct_answer: A. Excessive intestinal absorption of iron with deposition in organs
why_correct: Hereditary haemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder, most often due to homozygous C282Y HFE mutation, in which low hepcidin activity allows unregulated absorption of iron from the gut. The excess iron is deposited in the liver, pancreas, skin, heart, joints and pituitary, producing cirrhosis, diabetes and skin pigmentation.
why_wrong: B. Impaired biliary copper excretion is the mechanism of Wilson disease. C. Unconjugated bilirubin accumulation occurs in haemolysis or Gilbert syndrome. D. Autoimmune damage to small bile ducts describes primary biliary cholangitis. E. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema and liver disease without skin pigmentation or diabetes.
pearl: Venesection is the first-line treatment and, if started before cirrhosis develops, gives a normal life expectancy.
thinking: Diabetes, skin pigmentation and hepatomegaly ↓ Homozygous C282Y HFE mutation ↓ Hereditary haemochromatosis ↓ Unregulated gut iron absorption ↓ Iron deposition in organs
exam_trap: B, Defective biliary copper excretion — both are inherited metal storage disorders affecting the liver, but copper overload is Wilson disease, not haemochromatosis.
takeaway: Hereditary haemochromatosis is iron overload from excessive gut absorption, with deposition in liver, pancreas and skin.

stem:
A 19-year-old woman is referred by her GP with a new tremor, slurred speech and deranged liver tests. On slit-lamp examination, the ophthalmologist sees a golden-brown band at the outer edge of each cornea.

What is this eye sign called?
why_correct: Kayser-Fleischer rings are golden-brown deposits of copper in Descemet's membrane at the corneal margin. In a young person with liver disease and neurological features such as tremor and dysarthria they strongly suggest Wilson disease. They are present in almost all patients with neurological involvement and are best seen on slit-lamp examination.
why_wrong: B. Corneal arcus is a grey-white lipid ring, seen with ageing or hyperlipidaemia. C. Bitot spots are foamy conjunctival patches due to vitamin A deficiency. D. Roth spots are retinal haemorrhages with pale centres, classically in endocarditis. E. A cherry-red spot is a macular finding seen in central retinal artery occlusion and some storage disorders.
pearl: Wilson disease is confirmed with a low serum caeruloplasmin, raised 24-hour urinary copper and, if needed, liver copper measurement.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Neurological signs with liver disease ↓ Golden-brown corneal margin ring ↓ Copper deposition in the cornea ↓ Kayser-Fleischer ring
exam_trap: B, Corneal arcus — it is also a ring at the corneal margin, but it is grey-white lipid and is not linked with liver or neurological disease.
takeaway: A golden-brown corneal margin ring in a young person with liver and neurological disease is a Kayser-Fleischer ring of Wilson disease.

stem:
A 16-year-old boy is brought to clinic by his parents because his school work has deteriorated, he has become irritable, and his handwriting has become shaky. Blood tests show raised transaminases and a low serum caeruloplasmin.

Build-up of which substance is responsible for his illness?
why_correct: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of the ATP7B copper transporter, which impairs incorporation of copper into caeruloplasmin and its excretion into bile. Copper accumulates in the liver, then in the brain and cornea, causing hepatitis, psychiatric change and movement disorders in young people. Treatment is with a copper chelator such as penicillamine or trientine, or with zinc, which reduces copper absorption from the gut.
why_wrong: B. Iron overload causes haemochromatosis, usually presenting in middle age with diabetes and pigmentation. C. Lead poisoning causes abdominal pain, anaemia and neuropathy but not low caeruloplasmin. D. Calcium accumulation is not the mechanism of this disease. E. Bilirubin may rise in liver disease but is not the underlying cause.
pearl: Wilson disease should be considered in anyone under about 40 with unexplained liver disease, or with liver disease plus neuropsychiatric symptoms.
thinking: Teenager with behavioural change and tremor ↓ Raised transaminases ↓ Low caeruloplasmin ↓ Wilson disease ↓ Copper accumulation
exam_trap: B, Iron — haemochromatosis is the more familiar metal storage liver disease, but it presents in middle age and does not lower caeruloplasmin.
takeaway: Wilson disease is copper accumulation from impaired biliary excretion, affecting liver, brain and cornea.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_correct: zinc reworded as reducing copper absorption, not listed as a chelator

stem:
On the surgical assessment unit, a 74-year-old man has noticed his eyes turning yellow over the past fortnight. He also reports troublesome itching, cola-coloured urine and clay-coloured stools. Bloods reveal a very high alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, with transaminases only slightly above normal.

How is this pattern of liver blood tests best described?
why_correct: A predominant rise in alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin with only modestly raised transaminases is a cholestatic pattern. Pale stools, dark urine and itch indicate that conjugated bilirubin and bile salts are not reaching the bowel. The next step is an ultrasound to look for bile duct dilatation, which distinguishes extrahepatic obstruction from intrahepatic cholestasis.
why_wrong: B. A hepatocellular pattern is dominated by raised ALT and AST. C. Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin with normal ALP and dark stools rather than pale. D. Synthetic failure is shown by a raised INR and low albumin. E. Gilbert syndrome causes mild isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal enzymes and urine.
pearl: Itch in cholestasis is relieved first-line with colestyramine, and resolves once the obstruction is relieved.
thinking: Jaundice with itch ↓ Dark urine and pale stools ↓ Very high ALP and bilirubin ↓ Transaminases only mildly raised ↓ Cholestatic pattern
exam_trap: B, Hepatocellular — transaminases are mildly raised so it is tempting, but the dominant abnormality is ALP and bilirubin.
takeaway: Predominantly raised ALP and bilirubin with pale stools and dark urine is a cholestatic pattern.

stem:
A 49-year-old man who drinks heavily every day presents to the emergency department with two weeks of jaundice, a tender enlarged liver and a low-grade fever. Alcohol-related hepatitis is suspected.

Which liver blood test finding would most support this diagnosis?

options.A: ALT raised far more than AST
options.B: Raised unconjugated bilirubin with entirely normal enzymes
options.D: AST raised to a greater degree than ALT

correct_answer: D. AST raised to a greater degree than ALT
why_correct: Alcohol-related liver injury characteristically raises AST more than ALT, typically with a ratio of about two or more. Transaminases are usually only moderately raised, and GGT is typically high. Jaundice with tender hepatomegaly and fever in a heavy drinker, together with this pattern, supports alcohol-related hepatitis, whose severity is assessed with scores such as the Glasgow alcoholic hepatitis score.
why_wrong: A. ALT predominance is more typical of viral or drug-induced hepatitis. B. Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia suggests haemolysis or Gilbert syndrome. C. Transaminases in the thousands suggest ischaemic, viral or paracetamol injury rather than alcohol. E. GGT is typically raised with heavy alcohol use.
pearl: Alcohol depletes pyridoxal phosphate, which ALT depends on more than AST, partly explaining the AST-dominant pattern.
thinking: Heavy daily alcohol ↓ Jaundice, tender hepatomegaly and fever ↓ Suspected alcohol-related hepatitis ↓ Alcohol injury raises AST more than ALT ↓ AST greater than ALT
exam_trap: C, Transaminases in the thousands — severe illness suggests huge enzymes, but in alcohol-related hepatitis transaminases are only modestly raised.
takeaway: Alcohol-related hepatitis typically shows AST raised more than ALT with only modestly raised transaminases.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman has felt tired for several months. Her GP finds that her ALT and AST are persistently raised with a normal alkaline phosphatase. Viral hepatitis serology is negative, anti-smooth muscle antibodies are positive and her immunoglobulin G is high. She also has vitiligo.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Autoimmune hepatitis typically affects young women and causes a hepatocellular pattern with raised transaminases. Positive anti-smooth muscle or antinuclear antibodies with a raised IgG are characteristic, and other autoimmune conditions such as vitiligo are commonly associated. Liver biopsy confirms the diagnosis and treatment is with corticosteroids and azathioprine.
why_wrong: A. Primary biliary cholangitis is cholestatic, with raised ALP and antimitochondrial antibodies. B. Primary sclerosing cholangitis is cholestatic and associated with IBD. C. Wilson disease can cause hepatitis in young people but not autoantibodies with raised IgG. D. Gilbert syndrome causes isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal enzymes.
pearl: Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis is associated with ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibodies; type 2, mostly in children, with anti-LKM1 antibodies.
thinking: Young woman with fatigue ↓ Hepatocellular pattern, normal ALP ↓ Viral serology negative ↓ Anti-smooth muscle antibodies and raised IgG ↓ Autoimmune hepatitis
exam_trap: A, Primary biliary cholangitis — it is the best-known autoimmune liver disease in women, but it is cholestatic and AMA-positive, unlike this hepatitic picture.
takeaway: Raised transaminases with autoantibodies and high IgG in a young woman suggest autoimmune hepatitis.

stem:
For six weeks a 22-year-old woman has been taking a slimming product she ordered from a website. Her sister now notices she looks yellow, and her GP arranges bloods: both transaminases are hugely elevated, but alkaline phosphatase is barely above its reference range.

How should this pattern of liver injury be classified?
why_correct: Marked elevation of ALT and AST out of proportion to ALP indicates hepatocellular injury, meaning damage to hepatocytes themselves. Herbal and dietary supplements are a recognised cause of drug-induced liver injury of this type. The supplement should be stopped, and her INR checked to assess synthetic function.
why_wrong: B. Cholestatic injury is dominated by raised ALP and GGT. C. Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin without large transaminase rises. D. Synthetic failure is shown by INR and albumin, not transaminases. E. Infiltrative processes such as malignancy typically cause a disproportionate rise in ALP.
pearl: Always ask about herbal remedies, supplements and over-the-counter medicines in unexplained liver injury, as patients often do not regard them as medicines.
thinking: Jaundice after a new supplement ↓ ALT and AST many times normal ↓ ALP only slightly raised ↓ Transaminase-dominant picture ↓ Hepatocellular injury
exam_trap: B, Cholestatic — jaundice makes cholestasis tempting, but jaundice occurs in both patterns and the enzyme ratio here is clearly transaminase-dominant.
takeaway: Transaminases raised far more than ALP indicate a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury.

stem:
A 41-year-old man has itching and tiredness, and his liver tests are cholestatic. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography shows a beaded appearance, with alternating short strictures and dilated segments in bile ducts both inside and outside the liver.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Multifocal strictures with intervening dilatation, giving a beaded appearance throughout the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary tree, are the hallmark of primary sclerosing cholangitis. MRCP is the first-line diagnostic test. He should also be assessed for inflammatory bowel disease, which coexists in most patients.
why_wrong: A. Primary biliary cholangitis affects the small intrahepatic ducts, so MRCP of the larger ducts is normal. B. A duct stone causes a filling defect with upstream dilatation, not multifocal stricturing. C. Cholangiocarcinoma typically causes a single dominant stricture, although it is a complication of PSC. E. Autoimmune hepatitis causes a hepatitic picture without bile duct strictures.
pearl: PSC carries a substantial lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma, and a new dominant stricture or rapid deterioration should raise this concern.
thinking: Itch with cholestatic liver tests ↓ MRCP shows multiple strictures with dilatation ↓ Beading of intra- and extrahepatic ducts ↓ Chronic stricturing biliary inflammation ↓ Primary sclerosing cholangitis
exam_trap: C, Cholangiocarcinoma — biliary strictures suggest malignancy, but a diffuse beaded pattern rather than a single dominant stricture indicates PSC.
takeaway: A beaded biliary tree with multifocal strictures on MRCP indicates primary sclerosing cholangitis.

stem:
Pre-operative bloods for an elective hernia repair in a 60-year-old man come back with only one abnormality: a high alkaline phosphatase. Bilirubin and transaminases are within range and he feels well.

To decide whether liver or bone is the source, which blood test should be added?
why_correct: Alkaline phosphatase comes mainly from the liver and bone. GGT is produced by the hepatobiliary system but not by bone, so a raised GGT alongside ALP indicates a hepatobiliary source, whereas a normal GGT points towards bone. This guides whether to pursue liver imaging or bone causes such as Paget disease.
why_wrong: A. Calcium may be abnormal in some bone diseases but does not establish the source of ALP. C. Creatine kinase reflects muscle damage. D. Amylase is used in pancreatic disease. E. Ferritin assesses iron stores and is an acute-phase reactant.
pearl: Alkaline phosphatase is physiologically raised in pregnancy (placental) and in growing adolescents (bone).
thinking: Isolated raised ALP ↓ Main sources are liver and bone ↓ GGT is hepatobiliary but not bony ↓ Raised GGT means liver source ↓ Check GGT
exam_trap: A, Serum calcium — it seems a natural bone test, but it is often normal in bone causes such as Paget disease and cannot localise the ALP.
takeaway: A raised GGT alongside a raised ALP indicates a hepatobiliary source rather than bone.

stem:
A 66-year-old man who takes naproxen for knee osteoarthritis tells the out-of-hours GP that since yesterday his stools have been jet black, sticky like tar and unusually foul-smelling.

Which term describes these stools?
why_correct: Melaena is black, tarry, offensive stool caused by blood that has been digested during passage through the gut. It usually indicates bleeding from the upper gastrointestinal tract, and NSAID-induced peptic ulceration is a common cause. He needs urgent assessment, including haemodynamic status and a Glasgow-Blatchford score.
why_wrong: B. Haematochezia is fresh red or maroon blood per rectum. C. Steatorrhoea is pale, bulky, greasy stool from fat malabsorption. D. Tenesmus is a feeling of incomplete rectal emptying. E. Haematemesis is vomiting of blood.
pearl: Oral iron and bismuth turn stools black, but these stools are formed rather than sticky and tarry and lack the offensive smell of melaena.
thinking: Black, tarry, foul-smelling stool ↓ Digested blood ↓ Usually upper GI source ↓ NSAID use suggests peptic ulcer ↓ Melaena
exam_trap: B, Haematochezia — it also means blood in the stool, but describes fresh red blood rather than black digested blood.
takeaway: Black, tarry, offensive stool is melaena and usually signals an upper gastrointestinal bleed.
notes: Reviewer fix: pearl: replaced awkward iron/bismuth sentence with clear distinguishing features from melaena

stem:
Over the past two months a 30-year-old man has noticed that his stools have become pale and oily, float in the pan and are very hard to flush away. He has also lost weight despite eating normally.

Which term best describes his stool abnormality?
why_correct: Steatorrhoea is excess fat in the stool, producing pale, bulky, greasy, offensive stools that float and are difficult to flush. Combined with weight loss it indicates fat malabsorption or maldigestion, for example from pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, coeliac disease or bile acid deficiency, which then needs investigating.
why_wrong: B. Melaena is black, tarry stool from digested blood. C. Haematochezia is fresh blood passed per rectum. D. Tenesmus is the sensation of incomplete rectal emptying. E. Haematemesis is vomiting of blood.
pearl: Faecal elastase is a simple stool test for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, a common cause of steatorrhoea.
thinking: Pale, oily, floating stools ↓ Difficult to flush ↓ Weight loss ↓ Fat not being absorbed ↓ Steatorrhoea
exam_trap: D, Tenesmus — it is another stool-related term, but it describes a sensation of incomplete emptying, not the appearance of the stool.
takeaway: Pale, greasy, floating, hard-to-flush stools with weight loss describe steatorrhoea from fat malabsorption.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman with known gallstones comes to the emergency department after a large meal. She has sudden, constant upper abdominal pain that bores through to her back and she cannot stop vomiting. Bloods have been sent.

Which combination of findings would establish the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?

options.A: Upper abdominal tenderness together with a raised C-reactive protein
options.B: A pancreatic enzyme level only slightly above the upper limit of normal
options.C: Characteristic pain together with a markedly raised serum lipase or amylase
options.D: Pyrexia, a raised white cell count and persistent vomiting
options.E: Jaundice with a raised bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase

correct_answer: C. Characteristic pain together with a markedly raised serum lipase or amylase
why_correct: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when typical pain is accompanied by a markedly raised pancreatic enzyme, or by characteristic imaging findings. Her sudden boring epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting is the classic picture, so a clearly elevated lipase or amylase confirms it. Lipase stays raised for longer and is slightly more specific than amylase.
why_wrong: A. A raised CRP and tenderness reflect inflammation of any cause and do not identify the pancreas. B. A marginal enzyme rise is non-specific and occurs in many abdominal emergencies. D. Fever, leucocytosis and vomiting are non-specific features of many acute abdominal conditions. E. This pattern suggests biliary obstruction or cholangitis rather than confirming pancreatitis.
pearl: CRP measured around 48 hours after onset is a useful marker of severity in acute pancreatitis, but it plays no part in making the diagnosis.
thinking: Sudden epigastric pain boring to the back with vomiting ↓ Known gallstones raise suspicion of pancreatitis ↓ Diagnosis needs typical pain plus enzymes or imaging ↓ Only a marked rise in lipase or amylase is meaningful ↓ Typical pain with a markedly raised enzyme confirms it
exam_trap: B, A pancreatic enzyme only slightly above normal — any rise in amylase looks supportive, but small rises occur in perforation, ischaemic bowel and other emergencies, so only a marked elevation counts.
takeaway: Acute pancreatitis is confirmed by typical pain plus a markedly raised lipase or amylase, or by characteristic imaging.

stem:
Over two days, a 58-year-old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis has become drowsy, sleeps through the day and is muddled about the date, so her husband brings her to the GP surgery. He mentions she has not opened her bowels for almost a week. There is no fever and she has not vomited blood.

What is the most likely trigger for her deterioration?

options.B: Cutting down on salt in her diet

why_correct: Hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis is often provoked by an identifiable trigger, and constipation is one of the commonest. Prolonged retention of stool increases the gut-derived nitrogenous load reaching a liver that cannot clear it. Her week without a bowel movement, with no signs of infection or bleeding, makes constipation the likely cause, and treatment includes lactulose titrated to two to three soft stools a day.
why_wrong: A. Gentle exercise does not precipitate encephalopathy. B. Salt restriction is part of managing ascites and is not a trigger. C. Extra water intake does not cause encephalopathy; dehydration or overdiuresis would. E. Routine vitamin supplements are not a recognised precipitant.
pearl: Common precipitants of hepatic encephalopathy include infection (including spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), gastrointestinal bleeding, constipation, dehydration or overdiuresis, electrolyte disturbance and sedative drugs.
thinking: Cirrhosis with new drowsiness and confusion ↓ Suspect hepatic encephalopathy ↓ Look for a precipitant ↓ No fever or bleeding reported ↓ Week without bowel opening points to constipation
exam_trap: B, Cutting down on salt — changes in diet feel relevant in liver disease, but salt restriction treats ascites and does not provoke encephalopathy.
takeaway: Constipation is a common and easily treated trigger of hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis.

stem:
On a medical ward, a 70-year-old man with known cirrhosis has become disorientated and has a flapping tremor. His stool chart shows no bowel opening for four days since admission, and an infection screen is negative. The registrar asks the foundation doctor how the lack of bowel opening could explain his worsening mental state.

Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: A distended bowel compresses the portal vein and reduces liver blood flow
options.B: Faecal loading reduces carbohydrate absorption and causes hypoglycaemia
options.C: Straining at stool raises intracranial pressure
options.D: Slower colonic transit lets gut bacteria produce more ammonia, which is absorbed into the portal circulation
options.E: Retained stool releases toxins that cause acute hepatocyte necrosis

correct_answer: D. Slower colonic transit lets gut bacteria produce more ammonia, which is absorbed into the portal circulation
why_correct: Colonic bacteria break down protein and urea to produce ammonia and other nitrogenous compounds. When transit slows, more of these are generated and absorbed, and a cirrhotic liver with portosystemic shunting cannot clear them, so they reach the brain. This is why lactulose, which speeds transit and acidifies the colon to trap ammonia, is the first-line treatment.
why_wrong: A. Stool in the colon does not meaningfully compress the portal vein. B. Constipation does not reduce carbohydrate absorption enough to cause hypoglycaemia. C. Straining causes only brief pressure changes and does not explain encephalopathy. E. Constipation does not directly cause hepatocyte necrosis or acute liver failure.
pearl: Lactulose is converted by colonic bacteria to acids that lower colonic pH, converting ammonia to non-absorbable ammonium; rifaximin is added to prevent recurrence.
thinking: Cirrhosis with confusion and asterixis ↓ No bowel opening for several days ↓ Gut bacteria generate ammonia from nitrogenous material ↓ Slow transit increases production and absorption ↓ Failing liver and shunting let ammonia reach the brain
exam_trap: A, Compression of the portal vein — portal pressure is central to cirrhosis so a mechanical explanation sounds plausible, but the problem is increased ammonia load, not reduced liver blood flow.
takeaway: Constipation worsens hepatic encephalopathy by increasing gut ammonia production and absorption.

stem:
On a gastroenterology ward round, a 63-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis is asked to hold both arms out straight with her wrists bent back and fingers spread. After a few seconds her hands repeatedly drop forward and then jerk back up into position.

What is the name of this sign?
why_correct: Asterixis is a coarse flapping movement seen when the wrists are held dorsiflexed; it results from brief lapses in sustained muscle tone (negative myoclonus). In a patient with decompensated cirrhosis it is a classic sign of hepatic encephalopathy. It is elicited exactly as described, with the arms outstretched and the wrists extended.
why_wrong: A. Intention tremor worsens as a limb approaches a target and indicates cerebellar disease. B. Dysdiadochokinesia is impaired rapid alternating movements, also cerebellar. D. Pronator drift is slow pronation and downward drift of an arm with the palms up, indicating an upper motor neurone lesion. E. Clonus is rhythmic contractions after sudden stretching of a muscle and is not tested with the arms outstretched.
pearl: Asterixis is not specific to liver failure: it also occurs in uraemia and carbon dioxide retention.
thinking: Arms outstretched with wrists dorsiflexed ↓ Hands drop and jerk back repeatedly ↓ Lapses of postural tone, not a true tremor ↓ Patient has decompensated cirrhosis ↓ This is asterixis, a sign of hepatic encephalopathy
exam_trap: A, Intention tremor — the movement looks like a tremor, but intention tremor appears on reaching for a target, whereas asterixis appears while holding a fixed posture.
takeaway: A flapping movement of the outstretched dorsiflexed hands is asterixis, classically seen in hepatic encephalopathy.

stem:
At his inflammatory bowel disease clinic, a 34-year-old man with ulcerative proctitis says that several times a day he feels he must rush to the toilet and strain, yet passes only a small amount of mucus and blood and is left feeling that his rectum is still not empty.
