What is the term for this symptom?
why_correct: Tenesmus is a persistent or repeated urge to defecate with a feeling of incomplete evacuation, often with little or no stool passed. It reflects inflammation or a mass in the rectum, which is why it is typical of proctitis. His repeated straining with scanty output and a sense of a full rectum fits this exactly.
why_wrong: A. Steatorrhoea is pale, bulky, greasy stool from fat malabsorption. C. Haematochezia means passing fresh blood per rectum, which he has, but it does not describe the urge and sense of incomplete emptying. D. Odynophagia is pain on swallowing. E. Encopresis is involuntary passage of stool, usually used for children with overflow soiling.
pearl: New tenesmus in an older adult should prompt assessment for rectal cancer, as a rectal mass can produce the same sensation as inflammation.
thinking: Repeated urgent urge to open bowels ↓ Little passed despite straining ↓ Feeling the rectum is not empty ↓ Known rectal inflammation ↓ Symptom is tenesmus
exam_trap: C, Haematochezia — he does pass blood, so this is tempting, but the question asks for the name of the urge with incomplete evacuation, which is tenesmus.
takeaway: A frequent urge to defecate with a sense of incomplete emptying and little stool passed is tenesmus.

presentation: Red flag features in suspected IBS
stem:
Years ago a 49-year-old woman was told she had irritable bowel syndrome. She now visits her GP because, over the last three months, her crampy lower abdominal pain has returned with looser stools, she has lost weight without trying and she has noticed blood mixed in with her stool.

Why is it inappropriate to put her current symptoms down to irritable bowel syndrome?

options.A: Unintentional weight loss and rectal bleeding are red flag features that need investigation for organic disease
options.B: Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause abdominal pain
options.C: Irritable bowel syndrome cannot be diagnosed in anyone over 40
options.D: Irritable bowel syndrome usually causes fever and raised inflammatory markers
options.E: Irritable bowel syndrome never causes loose stools

correct_answer: A. Unintentional weight loss and rectal bleeding are red flag features that need investigation for organic disease
why_correct: Irritable bowel syndrome does not explain unintentional weight loss or rectal bleeding. These are red flag features that should prompt assessment for colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease and other organic disease, including FIT testing and referral under NICE suspected cancer guidance where criteria are met. A previous label of IBS must not stop new alarm features from being investigated.
why_wrong: B. Abdominal pain is a core feature of irritable bowel syndrome. C. There is no upper age limit for the diagnosis, although new symptoms in older adults need extra caution. D. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause fever or raised inflammatory markers. E. Loose stools are common in diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome.
pearl: Before diagnosing irritable bowel syndrome, NICE advises checking a full blood count, ESR or CRP and coeliac serology, and faecal calprotectin when inflammatory bowel disease is possible.
thinking: Previous diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome ↓ New weight loss without trying ↓ Blood mixed with stool ↓ These are not explained by a functional disorder ↓ Treat as red flags and investigate
exam_trap: E, IBS never causes loose stools — it sounds like a reason to doubt the diagnosis, but diarrhoea is common in IBS; the real concern is the weight loss and bleeding.
takeaway: Weight loss or rectal bleeding in someone labelled with IBS are red flags that need investigating, not reassurance.

stem:
A 27-year-old man has had bloating and cramping lower abdominal pain on and off for a year. The pain eases after he opens his bowels, and he swings between constipation and loose motions. He asks his GP whether this could be something more serious.

Which additional feature in his history would most suggest inflammatory bowel disease rather than irritable bowel syndrome?

options.A: Pain that is relieved by defecation
options.C: Ongoing blood mixed with his stool
options.D: Bloating that worsens through the evening
options.E: Symptoms that flare at times of stress

correct_answer: C. Ongoing blood mixed with his stool
why_correct: Persistent rectal bleeding is not a feature of irritable bowel syndrome and suggests mucosal disease such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease. It should prompt blood tests, faecal calprotectin and referral rather than reassurance. The other features listed are all typical of irritable bowel syndrome.
why_wrong: A. Pain relieved by opening the bowels is one of the core features supporting irritable bowel syndrome. B. Passage of mucus is recognised in irritable bowel syndrome and is listed by NICE as a supportive feature. D. Bloating that worsens through the day is typical of irritable bowel syndrome. E. Stress commonly aggravates irritable bowel syndrome.
pearl: Faecal calprotectin helps separate inflammatory bowel disease from irritable bowel syndrome in adults with lower GI symptoms when cancer is not suspected.
thinking: Pain eased by defecation with altered habit ↓ Pattern fits irritable bowel syndrome ↓ Look for features that IBS does not explain ↓ Ongoing rectal bleeding implies mucosal disease ↓ Raise concern for inflammatory bowel disease
exam_trap: B, Passing mucus — mucus sounds like a sign of inflammation, but it is common in irritable bowel syndrome and does not by itself point to inflammatory bowel disease.
takeaway: Persistent rectal bleeding is a red flag that is not explained by irritable bowel syndrome.

stem:
For several months a 71-year-old woman has had intermittent cramping pain in her left iliac fossa and alternating constipation and loose motions. She is afebrile and well, and her inflammatory markers are normal. Because of her age and change in bowel habit she was referred on the suspected cancer pathway, and colonoscopy showed numerous outpouchings in the sigmoid colon with no tumour or mucosal inflammation.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Symptomatic diverticular disease describes diverticula causing recurrent abdominal pain and altered bowel habit without acute inflammation. She has no fever and normal inflammatory markers, and cancer has appropriately been excluded by colonoscopy, which showed sigmoid diverticula only. That combination fits diverticular disease rather than an acute inflammatory or obstructive process.
why_wrong: A. Acute diverticulitis causes constant pain with fever, tenderness and raised inflammatory markers. B. New-onset bowel symptoms at this age are not attributed to irritable bowel syndrome, and colonoscopy has found a structural explanation. D. Ischaemic colitis presents acutely with pain and bloody diarrhoea and abnormal mucosa on colonoscopy. E. Sigmoid volvulus causes acute distension, absolute constipation and vomiting.
pearl: NICE advises a high-fibre diet and simple analgesia such as paracetamol for diverticular disease, avoiding NSAIDs and opioids where possible because they increase the risk of perforation.
thinking: Older woman with new change in bowel habit ↓ Cancer excluded first by colonoscopy ↓ Sigmoid diverticula with no inflammation ↓ Afebrile with normal inflammatory markers ↓ Symptomatic diverticular disease
exam_trap: A, Acute diverticulitis — diverticula plus left iliac fossa pain trigger this reflex, but there is no fever, no raised inflammatory markers and no inflamed mucosa.
takeaway: Diverticula causing recurrent symptoms without inflammation is symptomatic diverticular disease, diagnosed only after cancer is excluded in older adults.

stem:
A 29-year-old teacher was recently diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome after normal blood tests, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin. At a follow-up appointment with her GP she asks whether the condition is damaging her bowel or could turn into cancer.

Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: It causes patchy inflammation through the full thickness of the bowel wall
options.B: It causes mucosal changes that increase the risk of bowel cancer
options.C: It is a disorder of gut function and sensitivity that does not damage the structure of the bowel
options.D: It gradually scars and narrows the colon over time
options.E: It produces shallow ulcers that bleed from time to time

correct_answer: C. It is a disorder of gut function and sensitivity that does not damage the structure of the bowel
why_correct: Irritable bowel syndrome is a disorder of gut-brain interaction, involving altered motility and heightened visceral sensitivity without inflammation, ulceration or structural damage. It does not increase the risk of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Explaining this clearly is an important part of management and helps reduce anxiety.
why_wrong: A. Patchy transmural inflammation describes Crohn's disease. B. Irritable bowel syndrome does not raise colorectal cancer risk. D. Fibrotic strictures occur with Crohn's disease or ischaemia, not irritable bowel syndrome. E. Mucosal ulceration and bleeding suggest inflammatory bowel disease.
pearl: First-line management of irritable bowel syndrome is lifestyle and dietary advice, with antispasmodics, laxatives or loperamide for predominant symptoms and low-dose tricyclics if these fail.
thinking: Diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome after normal tests ↓ Patient worried about bowel damage and cancer ↓ IBS is a functional disorder ↓ No inflammation, ulceration or stricturing ↓ No increased cancer risk
exam_trap: B, Mucosal changes raising cancer risk — long-term bowel conditions such as colitis do raise cancer risk, so this seems plausible, but irritable bowel syndrome causes no mucosal damage.
takeaway: Irritable bowel syndrome is a functional disorder that does not damage the bowel or increase cancer risk.

presentation: Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in older adults
stem:
Pre-operative bloods taken for a 74-year-old man before a planned hernia repair show a microcytic anaemia with a low ferritin. He eats a varied diet including red meat, takes no anticoagulants or antiplatelets, and has not noticed black motions or blood when he opens his bowels.

Which underlying cause must be ruled out?
why_correct: Iron deficiency anaemia in an older man with an adequate diet and no visible bleeding is assumed to be due to occult gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise. Colorectal and gastric cancers frequently bleed silently, so he needs referral on the suspected cancer pathway for upper and lower GI investigation. Coeliac serology should also be checked.
why_wrong: B. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic, not microcytic, anaemia. C. Anaemia of chronic disease usually gives a normal or raised ferritin. D. Thalassaemia trait causes microcytosis with normal iron stores. E. Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia.
pearl: In men of any age and in postmenopausal women, unexplained iron deficiency anaemia warrants both upper and lower GI investigation, because a lesion may be found at either end.
thinking: Microcytic anaemia with low ferritin ↓ Confirms true iron deficiency ↓ Diet adequate and no visible bleeding ↓ Older man, so occult GI loss is likely ↓ Exclude gastrointestinal cancer
exam_trap: C, Anaemia of chronic disease — common in older people and can be microcytic, but the low ferritin confirms absolute iron deficiency, which points to blood loss.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in an older adult must be investigated for gastrointestinal cancer.

presentation: Coeliac disease and refractory iron deficiency
stem:
For four months a 38-year-old woman has taken ferrous sulfate as prescribed, yet repeat bloods show her haemoglobin and ferritin are still low. Her periods are light and regular, she eats meat, and apart from occasional bloating she has no gut symptoms. She has noticed no blood loss.

Which underlying condition should be tested for?
why_correct: Iron deficiency that fails to respond to adequate oral iron suggests malabsorption, and coeliac disease is an important and common cause to exclude. Villous atrophy in the duodenum, where iron is absorbed, impairs uptake, and gut symptoms may be mild or absent. NICE recommends coeliac serology for anyone with unexplained iron deficiency anaemia.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids cause visible bright red bleeding, which she does not have. B. Reflux disease does not usually cause iron deficiency unless there is severe oesophagitis with bleeding. C. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause anaemia and would not explain failure to absorb iron. D. Chronic cholecystitis does not affect iron absorption.
pearl: Tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA is the first-line test for coeliac disease; if IgA deficient, an IgG-based test is used instead.
thinking: Iron deficiency not corrected by oral iron ↓ No menstrual or visible blood loss ↓ Think of poor absorption ↓ Iron is absorbed in the duodenum ↓ Test for coeliac disease
exam_trap: C, Irritable bowel syndrome — her bloating suggests a functional cause, but irritable bowel syndrome never explains anaemia, and coeliac disease must be excluded first.
takeaway: Iron deficiency that does not respond to oral iron should prompt testing for coeliac disease.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_correct: softened 'coeliac disease is the commonest cause in the UK' of refractory iron deficiency (unsupported; H. pylori, atrophic gastritis, PPI use and non-adherence also common) to 'an important and common cause to exclude'.
